parole.testo: Borrowed from French aorte, from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ).
Partial calque of French eau de Javel.
Borrowed from French abcès, from Latin abscessus.
Borrowed from French atrophie. Compare Turkish atrofi.
From آتش (âtaš, “fire”) + بس (bas, “enough; stop”), probably a calque of French cessez-le-feu or some other European language.

From French arsenic, from Latin arsenicum, from Late/Byzantine Greek ἀρσενικόν (arsenikón, “yellow arsenic”), from Classical Syriac ܙܪܢܝܟܐ (zarnīḵā), from Middle Persian *zarnīk, from Old Median *zaraniyakā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰelh₃-.

parole.significato: bow (used for playing various stringed musical instruments)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French aryen or English Aryan by Mirza Aqa Khan Kermani in the late 19th century. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Áryas. Doublet of ایر (ir, “Iranian”), which was inherited, and آریا (âriyâ, “Aryan”), which is a learned borrowing.
Borrowed from French asbeste, from Latin asbestos, from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos).
Borrowed from French album, from Latin album (“blank white writing tablet”).
Borrowed from French alternative, from Medieval Latin alternativus.
Borrowed from French améthyste, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀμέθυστος (améthustos, “not drunk”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μεθύω (methúō, “I am drunk”), from μέθυ (méthu, “wine”).
From French ananas, from Spanish ananás, Portuguese ananás, from Old Tupi naná (“pineapple”).
From French académie, from Latin acadēmīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀκαδημία (Akadēmía).
Borrowed from French acoustique or English acoustic, from Latin acousticus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓κουστῐκός (ăkoustĭkós).
Borrowed from French eau de Cologne.
Borrowed from French érosion. Compare Turkish erozyon.
Borrowed from French staphylocoque. By surface analysis, استافیلوـ (estâfilo-, “staphylo-”) + ـکوک (-kok, “-coccus”). Compare Turkish stafilokok.
Borrowed from French strepto-, from Ancient Greek στρεπτός (streptós, “twisted”). Compare Turkish strepto-.
Borrowed from French streptocoque. By surface analysis, استرپتوـ (esterepto-, “strepto-”) + ـکوک (-kok, “-coccus”). Compare Turkish streptokok.
Borrowed from French esparcet, esparcette, from Occitan esparceto or Spanish esparceta, possibly related to esparcir (“to scatter”).
Borrowed from French squelette. Compare Turkish iskelet.
Borrowed from French électron, from English electron.

Borrowed from French alcool, from Arabic الْكُحُل (al-kuḥul) (a direct boring from Arabic would drop the definite article ال (al-)), see there for more. Doublet of کحل (kuhl /kohl) and الکحل (alkuhul /alkohol).
Borrowed from French infarctus, from Latin īnfarctus.
Borrowed from French urologie. Compare Turkish üroloji.
Borrowed from French ulcère. Compare Turkish ülser.
Borrowed from French échocardiographie. Compare Turkish ekokardiyografi.

parole.significato: isolated; quarantined (e.g. of a hospital room, substance, etc..)
immune, relating to the immune system
parole.testo: Phono-semantic matching of French immun or English immune.
Borrowed from French bar, from Ancient Greek βᾰ́ρος (bắros).

Calqued from French hélicoptère. Composed of بال (bâl, “wing”) + گرد (gard, present stem of گردیدن (gardidan, “to rotate”)) Coined by the Academy of Persian Language and Literature as a replacement for هلیکوپتر.
Borrowed from French béton (“concrete”), from Latin bitūmen (“asphalt”).
Borrowed from French brosse. Doublet of فرچه (ferče, “shaving-brush; brush”).

parole.significato: Berlin (the capital and largest city of Germany)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French bronze, itself from Italian bronzo. See there for further information, but perhaps ultimately a twice-borrowed term from Persian برنج (berenj, “brass”) or Persian پرنگ (pereng, “copper”). Nowadays more common than older مفرغ (mefraġ), from Arabic.

parole.significato: theatre (a collaborative form of performing art)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French tramway, from English tramway.
Partial calque of French transaction, English transaction. By surface analysis, ترا + [script needed] (terâ-, “trans-”) + کنش (koneš, “action”).
Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from terreur, or pseudo-anglicism derived from terror.

From French tzar, from Russian царь (carʹ), from Old East Slavic цьсарь (cĭsarĭ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, from a Germanic language, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of قِیْصَر and سِزار.
Borrowed from French testicule, from Latin testiculus.
Borrowed from French télévision in Iran, or English television in Dari.

From تن (tan, present stem of تنیدن (tanidan, “to weave (a spider's web), to twist”)) + ـش (-eš). It is not found with the current meaning in early 1900s dictionaries (Steingass, Dehkhoda, Hayyim). It might be a phono-semantic matching of French tension or some other European language.
Borrowed from French toucan, borrowed from Old Tupi tukana, from Proto-Tupi-Guarani *tũkãn, from Proto-Tupian *jɨokãn.
Borrowed from French T, because the shape resembles the Roman letter T.
Pseudo-Gallicism, derived from titre + -age. Not related to French titrage (“titration”).

Modern partial calque of French khanat, itself a compound of khan + -at (modeled after terms like califat). Adapted into Iranian Persian as خانات (xânât) following a pattern of transcribing French -at as ـات (-ât), as seen in کنترات (kontorât) from French contrat. Older Persian terms for “khanate” i
Calque of French automobile, from خود (xod, “self”) + رو (row, “present stem of رفتن (raftan, “to go”)”).
From دامن (dâman, “skirt, hems of a robe”) + ـه (-e). "Domain; range" is a phono-semantic matching of French domaine.
Borrowed from French dermatologie. Compare Turkish dermatoloji.
Calque of French de seconde main or English secondhand.
From دست (dast, “hand”) + کار (kār/kâr, “work”) + ـی (-ī/i). The sense of manipulation is a semantic loan from French manipulation or a semantic loan from English manipulation.
Borrowed from French diligence (“stage-coach”), from Latin diligentia.

Borrowed from French démocratique, from Middle French democratique, from Late Latin democraticus, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐκός (dēmokrătĭkós, “of or for democracy; favouring or suited for democracy”), from δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā, “democracy”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, suffix with the sense ‘relating’ to
Borrowed from French démocratie, from Middle French democratie, from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā).
Borrowed from French démographie, from Ancient Greek δῆμος (dêmos) + γράφω (gráphō).
دو (do, “two”) + زیست (zist, “life”). Calque of French amphibie.
Borrowed from French dictionnaire. Doublet of Dari دکشنری (dikšinarī).
From French radio (Iranian Persian) or English radio (Dari).
From راه (râh) + آهن (âhan), after French chemin de fer.
Borrowing from French rose, from Latin rosa, possibly from Ancient Greek ῥόδον (rhódon), itself possibly from an Iranian language. Doublet of گل (gol) if the Greek is an Iranian borrowing.
Borrowed from French rhum or directly from English rum.
Partial calque of French rouge à lèvres.
Borrowed from French risque or English risk.
From French rimmel, ultimately from the name of the inventor of the first mascara product in the 19th century, Eugene Rimmel, and the cosmetics firm founded by him, Rimmel.
Borrowed from French rhino-, from Ancient Greek ῥινός (rhinós), genitive of ῥίς (rhís, “nose”).
Borrowed from French rhinopharyngite. By surface analysis, رینوـ (rino-, “rhino-”) + فارنژیت (fâranžit, “pharyngitis”).
Borrowed from French rhinoplastie. By surface analysis, رینوـ (rino-, “rhino-”) + ـپلاستی (-plâsti, “-plasty”).
From زیر (zir, “under”) + دریا (daryâ, “sea”) + ـی (-i). Calque of French sous-marin.
From زیر (zir, “under”) + ساخت (sâxt, “structure”). Presumably a calque of French infrastructure.
Borrowed from French cédille, from Spanish cedilla.
Borrowed from French seringue, from Medieval Latin sȳringa, from Classical Latin sȳrinx, from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx).

parole.significato: cell (the basic unit of a living organism)

parole.testo: Phono-semantic matching of French sphère and/or English sphere, from Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra), which is not originally related to etymology 1 above.
From سیب (“apple”) + زمینی (“earthly, from earth”), a calque of French pomme de terre.
Probably a calque of French aurore polaire.

parole.significato: knight; a warrior of the Middle Ages.

parole.testo: Borrowed from French cheminée. Compare Turkish şömine (“fireplace”).
Borrowed from French -logie, from Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογῐ́ᾱ (-logĭ́ā). Compare Turkish -loji.
Borrowed from French -coque, from New Latin coccus, from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed”). Compare Turkish -kok.

parole.significato: used to form nouns of action or process
faculty, staff (of a university or college)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French faculté. While associated with Dari, the term was likely borrowed via Iranian Persian based on the reinterpretation of a final /e/ as a short /a/.
Borrowed from French fer (“iron”). With the sense of "curly" specifically being a clipping of fer à lisser (“curling iron”).
From فرا (farâ-, “beyond”) + فکن (fekan, “to throw”) + ـی (-i). Calque of French projection or calque of English projection.
Borrowed from French fraction (“wing, faction”), from Latin fractio. The sense “parliamentary group” may be an influence from Russian фракция (frakcija) and/or German Fraktion.
Borrowed from French forme and English form.

parole.significato: A, La (the sixth note of the fixed-Do solfège scale)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French lycée, while more common in Dari, it was likely borrowed via Iranian Persian. Since Dari does not generally use a he to transcribe a final -e.
Borrowed from French macération. Compare Turkish maserasyon.
Possibly from French masque or English mask.
Calque of French machine à écrire.
Borrowed from French maman. Displaced ننه (nana /nane) in most urban dialects of Iran.

parole.significato: a woman’s coat or upper garment that can be worn in public without a chador (see usage note below)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French manteau during the Qajar period. The current usage originated in the 1970s.
Borrowed from French modèle and English model.
Borrowed from French Mauritanie, from Latin Mauritania.
Borrowed from French musique, from Old French musique, from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “art of the Muses”).

parole.significato: carpet (fabric used as a complete floor covering)
mechanic (a skilled worker in charge of maintenance or repairing machinery)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French miniature or English miniature.
Borrowed from French micro-organisme. By surface analysis, میکروـ (mikro-, “micro-”) + ارگانیسم (orgânism, “organism”).
Borrowed from French microbiologie. By surface analysis, میکروـ (mikro-, “micro-”) + بیولوژی (biyoloži, “biology”).
Borrowed from French microphone, from Ancient Greek μικρός (mikrós, “small”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”).
Likely borrowed from French natron, from Arabic نطرون
Calque of French noire (“quarter note”, literally “black”).
From نخست (nuxust, “first”) + ـی (-ī). Calque of French primate, which is from primas (“first”).
Borrowed from French neurologie. Compare Turkish nöroloji.
Phono-semantic matching of French homogène, based on a back-formation from همگنان (hamgenân, “fellowmen, peers”).
Borrowed from French variation. Compare Turkish varyasyon.

parole.significato: vafoor, bafoor, a type of opium pipe traditionally used in Iran and Afghanistan

parole.testo: Borrowed from French vagin, from Latin vāgīna.
Borrowed from French vésicule. Compare Turkish vezikül.
Borrowed from French vue or English view.
Borrowed from French parc or English park.
Borrowed from French papillon (“butterfly”), short for nœud papillon (“bow tie”).
Borrowed from French paquet. Compare Ottoman Turkish پاكت.
Borrowed from French procès, from Latin processus.
Borrowed from French programme, from Latin programma.
Borrowed from French pneumothorax. By surface analysis, پنوموـ (penomo-, “pneumo-”) + توراکس (torâks, “thorax”). Compare Turkish pnömotoraks.
Borrowed from French pneumo-, from Ancient Greek πνεύμων (pneúmōn, “lung”). Compare Turkish pnömo-.
Borrowed from French pneumologie. By surface analysis, پنوموـ (penomo-, “pneumo-”) + ـلوژی (-loži, “-logy”). Compare Turkish pnömoloji.
Borrowed from French pneumonie, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía). Compare Turkish pnömoni.
Borrowed from French pneumocoque. By surface analysis, پنوموـ (penomo-, “pneumo-”) + ـکوک (-kok, “-coccus”). Compare Turkish pnömokok.
Borrowed from French piste. Compare Turkish pist.
Borrowed from French gène, from German Gen. From the same Proto-Indo-European root comes Persian زادن (zâdan, “to birth, to beget”).
Borrowed from French caducée, from Latin cādūceum, cādūceus.
Borrowed from French carte, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs), of further disputed origin.
Borrowed from French cardiologie. Compare Turkish kardiyoloji.
Borrowed from French café. Doublet of قهوه (qahve).

parole.significato: canal (waterway used for transportation of vessels)

parole.testo: Partial calque of French code postal.
Borrowed from French cravate. Doublet of کروات (korovât, “Croat”).

parole.significato: Crete (an island in the Mediterranean, and the largest in Greece)

parole.testo: From French chlore, derived from English chlorine, from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”) + -ine.
کلید (kelid, “key”) + ـی (-i). Probably a calque of French clé or a calque of English key.

parole.significato: coma, a prolonged state of unconsciousness

parole.testo: Borrowed from French commandant. Doublet of synonymous Dari قومَنْدَان (qōmandān).

parole.significato: commission (fee charged by an agent or broker for carrying out a transaction)
Konkur (the national university entrance examination in Iran)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French concours. Doublet of Dari کَانْکور (kānkōr).
Borrowed from French congrès, from Latin congressus. As a proper noun, a calque of English Congress.

parole.significato: curettage, D and C or D&C
Commagene (an ancient Greco-Iranian kingdom in northeastern Anatolia, modern Turkey, with a capital at Samosata)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Commagène, borrowed from Latin Commagēna, borrowed from Ancient Greek Κομμαγηνή (Kommagēnḗ).

parole.significato: copy (both the activity and the result)

parole.testo: Borrowed from French kiosque. Doublet of کوشْک.
Borrowed from French gaze or English gauze.

Learned borrowing from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐎡𐎹 (a-r-i-y /⁠Aryaʰ⁠/) or Avestan 𐬀𐬌𐬭𐬌𐬌𐬋 (aⁱriiō), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Áryas (see for more information). Doublet of ایر (êr, “Iranian”), which was inherited via Middle Persian 𐭠𐭩𐭫 (ʾyl /⁠ēr⁠/). Compare Urdu آریہ (ārya, “Aryan”). Attested in the Ne
Either from French idéologique or English ideologic.
From French billet, either directly with a spelling pronunciation or through Russian билет (bilet).
Borrowed from French tonne (in Iran) or from English ton (in Dari).
From either English syrup or French sirop. Doublet of شربت (šarbat) and سوربه (sorbe, “sorbet”).

parole.significato: E, Mi (the third note of the fixed-Do solfège scale)
parole.testo: Ultimately Borrowed from Latin mīra, either via French mi or English mi.
